new_statements.quote: 4.1. Gesogo is a language with lexical tone. The alternance of tone on verbal radicals is hidden in the infinitive, but is regularly observed in both affirmative and negative tenses. 4.2. Nominals can be classified into four tone-groups according to the tone of the radical and suffix. 4.3. The tone-pattern of words is maintained in all observed syntactical positions. 4.4. An acute accent (´) marks a high tone, and an unmarked syllable denotes a normal low tone. A circumflex accent (^) indicates a falling tone, and an inverted circumflex accent denotes a rising tone. A mid-tone is a slipped high tone and is marked with a grave accent (`).
new_statements.citation: Harries, Lyndon. 1955. Grammar of Gesogo. Kongo-Overzee 21(5): 420-440.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The language has lexical tone (high, low, falling, rising, and a 'slipped high' mid tone); nouns fall into four tone classes by radical+suffix tone and word tone patterns are stable across syntactic positions. No word stress is described anywhere in the sketch; the only 'accents' are tone diacritics. Stoop 1989 (pp. 130, 132) independently treats the language as H/L tonal with floating tones and says the tone of nominal prefixes could not yet be determined.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone: verbal-radical tone alternance is hidden in the infinitive; vowel length is grammatical, not lexical (§2.5).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone patterns of nouns and verb forms, elicited from one informant (Pierre Lifenya, chefferie Baluolambi, at Yakusu, Dec. 1954); tone patterns are said to hold in all observed syntactic positions.
new_statements.identity_note: Identity needs third reading. Harries 1955 describes 'Gesogo (ligesögo)' of the chefferie Baluolambi (chef-lieu Yonange, Yakusu area, south bank of the Congo west of Kisangani to the Lomami) and states on p. 420 'The language is also known as Topoke or Eso'; Stoop 1989 labels his 'sogo' Guthrie C53 and calls it 'le système sogo ou poke' (p. 128) — in Guthrie, C53 is Poke/Topoke while So(ko) of Basoko is C52. Glottolog/hh nevertheless map both Harries 1955 and Stoop 1989 to sode1235 [soc] (EBALL keyword c.52). So the quoted statement may describe Poke/Topoke [pof] = poke1238 rather than So of Basoko; Carrington's 'Baso/Heso' notes (Basoko variety) are the only material here unambiguously from So proper, and they contain no statement. Motingea 2012 (Basoa) is the source that would settle this.

new_statements.quote: §2.2.4 Tons: La langue des Basoa atteste des tons simples et des tons complexes. [...] Phonologiquement, il n'existe donc que le ton haut et le ton bas. Sur le plan phonétique pourtant on peut percevoir trois tons simples: haut, moyen et bas. [...] Les exemples (34c) indiquent la valeur lexicale des tons en soa. c. moto 'homme' vs. motó 'tête' [...] mwélá 'fumée' vs. mwěla 'queue'. (p. 24) — §6.4 (regional, p. 243): Il s'agit, par exemple, en dehors de la tonologie d'un système de stresses (ou rythmique ?) consistant à « traîner » dans la réalisation de certaines unités prosodiques. Ce système n'a malheusement encore fait l'objet d'aucune étude.
new_statements.translation: §2.2.4 Tones: The language of the Basoa attests simple tones and complex tones. [...] Phonologically, then, there exist only the high tone and the low tone. Phonetically, however, one can perceive three simple tones: high, mid and low. [...] The examples in (34c) show the lexical value of tones in Soa: moto 'man' vs. motó 'head' [...] mwélá 'smoke' vs. mwěla 'tail'. (p. 24) — §6.4 (about the whole Congo-bend region, p. 243): It is, for example, apart from the tonology, a matter of a system of stresses (or rhythm?) consisting in 'dragging out' the realisation of certain prosodic units. This system has unfortunately not yet been the object of any study.

new_statements.relation_note: Language not in the catalog. The existing statement (Harries 1955, Gesogo: lexical tone, no stress statement) is of the same type — tone language, no word-stress statement — so Motingea agrees with it in type. But Motingea himself files Harries 1955 under tofoké C53 (p. 241) and lists 'les Tofoké, connus aussi sous les noms de Sogo et Eso (Harries 1955, Stoop 1989a, Stoop 1989b)' as the southern NEIGHBOURS of the Basoa (p. 15), so the Harries statement most likely belongs to Poke [pof] poke1238, and this Motingea sketch is the first the deciding source that is unambiguously about So/Soa C52. The p. 243 remark is a regional, hedged suggestion of a stress/rhythmic system and does not give a p…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Soa (of Ilondé) is a two-tone language (H vs. L phonologically; a phonetic mid = H realised before L; rising and falling tones arise from vowel contraction or lexicalised consonant loss); tone is lexically contrastive (minimal pairs). The grammar sketch has no section on stress or accent and never states a stress placement; 'accent' occurs only as the name of the acute diacritic. The morphotoneme section describes tonal fusion, tone harmony, tonal polarity, métatonie (final -a of perfect/progressive raised before a following word, lowered phrase-finally, which the author calls 'prosodie phrasale'), Meeussen-type dissimilation, raising, a phonetic downstep of H between two L's ('faille tonale', °BHB > HMB), and a floating L in the prohibitive. The only mention of stress is a hedged regional remark in the closing chapter (p. 243) that the languages of the Congo bend up to the Batetela show, besides tone, a 'system of stresses (or rhythm?)' of lengthening certain prosodic units, never studied.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. Tonal notes: the young female informant Angèle Angwadima does not apply the tone-raising rule before connective/possessive (p. 38); the author cannot cleanly separate métatonie from the pausal low tone common to the Aruwimi-Lomamé languages (p. 36).
new_statements.identity_note: Motingea's ch. 2 describes 'la langue des Basoa telle qu'elle est parlée dans la localité d'Ilondé' (Secteur de Yawémbé, Territoire d'Isangi), the Basoa being 'connue aussi sous le nom de Basoko, Basɔkɔ́ selon la phonétique de la langue elle-même' (p. 15), = Guthrie C52 so (= soko) (p. 9); data from Ilongosi Ilonga of Ilondé (Mbandaka, Sept. 1993) checked with Marie Mondondi Mbuli and Angèle Angwandima of the same village (Kinshasa, Oct. 1999). The book's other sketches (Mbesa C51 [zms], Tofoké of Yangole C53 [pof], Lokelé of the Mboosó [khy]) are other languages. Motingea explicitly treats Tofoké = Sogo = Eso (Harries 1955, Stoop 1989a,b) as a neighbouring language, so the existing Harries 1955 statement filed under sode1235 most likely describes Poke [pof].

sources.note: 'Phonetic Data' (pp. 420-421: 7 vowels, grammatical vowel length) and 'Tonal Data' (p. 422): lexical tone language; nominals fall into four tone-groups; word tone-pattern maintained in all syntactic positions; H, L, falling, rising and mid ('slipped high') tones marked.
